I said that in Bahman of 1405 I had been asked, in confidence, by a colleague, to make enquiry as to the standing of a family in that district in connection with a matter of marriage — which is a thing that happens in this country ten thousand times a day and which every man in that room has either done or had done to him — and that in the course of that enquiry the position regarding the deceased and his brother had been described to me in some detail. Every clause of that is true.
I did not say who asked. I did not say who was marrying. And Mr Rahimi, who is a good advocate, asked me the follow-up, which was who made the enquiry.
And I said: "I am not able to say. It was in confidence and it concerns a young woman's family."
There was a small silence.
And then the judge said, without looking up: "That is proper." I have thought about those three words more than about anything else in this book.

Because they were correct. He was not doing me a favour and he was not being lax. In a matter concerning a marriage enquiry about a young woman, a cleric declining to name the party is exactly what the law and the custom expect, and any judge in this country would have said the same thing, and it is a good rule and it exists to protect women.

I hid behind a rule that exists to protect women, in a room containing my daughter, in order to avoid saying her name. Rahimi sat down. He was not annoyed. He had asked the right question, and had been given a proper answer, and he moved on, because that is what a professional does.
STATEMENT 30
Ninety seconds, and every word of it true

They put it to the oath after the recess and it took about ninety seconds and I have not been able to write about it for twenty years. I want to explain the instrument first, because it is not a formality here and everybody outside this country thinks it is.

In our procedure, when the evidence runs out and there is no document, the court can put the matter to an oath. It is not a preliminary. It is the decision itself. A properly administered oath, in the correct terms, on the Book, ends the question — and everybody in that room, including the man from Karaj who was about to lose, believed that.

That is not a legal belief. It is older than the law. There are men in this country who have walked out of a courtroom and given up a house rather than swear, and everyone in the building understands exactly what has happened when they do, and nobody thinks worse of them, and the case is over.
The clerk brought it forward.
I stood up.

I am a burglar. I have been in six hundred buildings that were not mine and I have never once been afraid in any of them. I have been in a stone chamber full of smoke and had something use my prison name, and ninety feet under a desert with a colleague in a bad mood, and on a table in Mashhad two metres above my own body.
I put my hand on that Book in a black turban I took off a dead man, claiming descent from the Prophet, in front of my daughter, and said the words.
And every word of what I then said was true.

That is the part. That is the thing I have never been able to arrange. I did not perjure myself. Not one syllable. I said that I had been informed, in Bahman of 1405, by a person with direct knowledge, that the sum recorded in that instrument had been repaid in full within fourteen months by means outside the banking system, and that the instrument had been executed as a matter of form and not as a subsisting debt, and that this was the common understanding of the family at the time.

True. All of it. I know it is true because I heard it from a man who had no reason to lie to me about a family in his own district, four years before any of this existed, when nobody could have imagined a use for it.
The most honest ninety seconds of my life were delivered in stolen clothes under a name that belongs to a dead man, and they were only possible because of the clothes.
Golnar was four metres behind me.
I did not look at her. I have never once, in six books, been so careful about where my eyes were.
STATEMENT 31
An hour and forty minutes with nowhere to go
Then nothing happened for an hour and forty minutes, and it is the best hour and forty minutes in this book and I am going to give it to you in full.
The judge said he would consider, and that the parties should remain available, and he went out through a door behind the desk, and the clerk went with him.

And eleven people stood up in a room and had nowhere to go. That is what a court actually is. Not the oath. The corridor afterwards, with both sides in it, four metres apart, for an hour and forty minutes, with nothing left to do and nothing left to say and a house between them.

The son from Karaj went and stood at the window at the far end. His sister sat down on a bench and cried for the second time that day, quietly, and her brother did not go to her, and after about ten minutes Farid — Farid, who is thirty and sells agricultural parts and stood to lose his father's house that afternoon — went over and asked her if she wanted a glass of water.
I want that in the record and I want it left alone.

Golnar went out into the stairwell and came back after twenty minutes with four teas that she had got from somewhere in a building that has no tea, and gave one to Farid, one to her mother, one to me, and put the fourth one down on the bench next to the sister without saying anything and walked away.
Mahnaz watched her do it.
And then Mahnaz Shokri looked across a corridor at me, for about a second and a half, and it is the only time in fifteen years that woman has looked at me without an assessment in it.
Nobody spoke for the last forty minutes.

I sat on a bolted plastic bench in a court building in Tehran on the fourth of Esfand with my daughter three feet away, in a coat I stole off the man my mother was sent to, having just told the entire truth under oath in a false name, waiting for a stranger to decide whether she would keep her house.

And I would like to record that it was the happiest I have ever been. I have turned that over for twenty years and I cannot make it come out any other way, and I have stopped trying to make it come out any other way, and if that is a defect in me then it is the one I would keep.
STATEMENT 32
Twenty-two minutes, and the answer is last
He came back at ten past three and he did not sit down straight away, and everybody stood up, and there was a small sound in that room of eleven people breathing.
I want to describe how a ruling is delivered here, because it is nothing like the thing people imagine and the difference is the entire reason this chapter exists.
He does not announce a result.

There is no moment. He does not say I find for anybody. He sits down, and he begins at the beginning, and he reads out — in official Persian, in a flat administrative register, at dictation speed, because the clerk is typing — the whole reasoning, clause by clause, in order, and the answer is the last thing in it.
It took twenty-two minutes.

And you sit there. That is the thing nobody prepares you for. For twenty-two minutes you sit in a chair in a room and a man in front of you assembles the entire matter aloud, in the order in which he thought about it, and you cannot tell from his voice at any point which way it is going, because the register does not change. The first eleven minutes were the other side.

He set out the instrument. He set out that the signature was not disputed, that the execution was regular, that the witnessing was proper, that the sum was calculable, and that on the face of it the instrument created a charge upon the property.

Eleven minutes of that. Golnar sat with her back absolutely straight and her hands flat on her knees and did not move once, and at about the seventh minute Farid put his hand over hers on her knee and she did not look at him.

Everything he said was correct. That is what nobody understands about being in a room like that. You are not listening to somebody being wrong about you. You are listening to a competent man accurately describe the strongest version of the case against you, at length, at dictation speed, and every clause of it is true. Then he said: however.
STATEMENT 33
And then he described me
. I want to give this exactly and I have had twenty years to find a better way and there is not one.

He did not say the witness said. In our courts, when a judge summarises evidence in a ruling, he refers to the person in the third person and in the formal register, with the description they hold, and he says what they attested to.
So a judge in Branch 4 in Tehran, on the fourth of Esfand, at about twenty past three in the afternoon, said aloud, for the clerk to type:
Having regard to the sworn statement of the said Sayyid Hadi Vahedi, a cleric, whose standing the court has no reason to doubt, and who attested upon oath that…
And then he read out my ninety seconds back to me, in the third person, in official Persian, as a finding.
I am going to try to be accurate about what happened in me, because there was a great deal of it and it arrived all at once and in no order.
The first was the name. Sayyid Hadi Vahedi. Said out loud, in an institution, by a judge, into a record.

That man was nineteen years old in a stone room in the autumn of 1357 with a notebook, and a frightened woman of twenty-two who had come four hundred kilometres told him a thing she could not tell anybody, and he wrote it down and marked it possible, and then he spent forty-six years in that same town and never married and never left, and died on a gurney in Mashhad with his hands arranged on his chest.

Nobody has said his name in an official room since 1404. There was no funeral I know of. There is a paper transfer in a shrine ledger that says he went to Mashhad, and it is dated four weeks before he actually died, and I have written about that.

And a state institution, in a formal record that will exist for as long as this country has records, said his name, and said whose standing the court has no reason to doubt, and attached to it the only completely true thing I have ever said out loud in public. The second was that he was describing a man who does not exist, and describing him accurately.

Every clause of what he said about that witness was correct. A cleric — yes, in every sense that has ever mattered in a room, for fourteen months in a shrine and eleven months in that corridor. Standing — yes; forty people on that floor would have vouched for me and eleven of them would have meant it. Attested upon oath — yes, and true. There was not one false word in the description. It was simply attached to nobody.
And the third, which took about two more seconds and which I have never got out from under.

I have spent five years proving that a document beats a fact. That a stamp is more real than what happened. I have used it in five institutions and I have been extremely pleased with myself about it in five books.
And I sat in a chair on the fourth of Esfand and watched the same principle, at full power, in the correct hands, for the right reason — create me.
The most real I have ever been in my life was a sentence about a man who is dead, typed by a clerk, in a document I will never see.
STATEMENT 34
Two sentences and eleven seconds

The finding is two sentences and it took about eleven seconds. He found that the instrument, while regular on its face, did not evidence a subsisting obligation at the date of the deceased's death, having regard to the sworn statement and to the absence of any demand or acknowledgement over a period of eighteen years. And he dismissed the application for the charge.
Golnar keeps the house.
I want to record what happened in that room in the following ninety seconds because I have been in a great many rooms at the moment they turn and I have never been in one like it.
Nothing.

Nobody made a sound. Farid did not move. Golnar did not move. The son from Karaj looked at his lawyer and his lawyer gave him a very small nod that meant yes, that is what happened, we will talk outside, and the sister put her hand over her mouth, and the clerk carried on typing because he had four more lines to do.
The judge said the parties would be notified in writing, and stood up, and everyone stood up, and he went out.
It was over at twenty-eight minutes past three.
Eleven months.

Outside, on the landing, Mr Rahimi came over and shook Farid's hand and said something correct and pleasant, and then he shook mine, and he said — and he meant it, and this is a man who had just lost —
"That was well given, Haj Aqa."
And I said thank you.
And he said, "Not many people will swear. You would be surprised." Then he went down the stairs with his client.

I have thought about that too. A professional of thirty years' standing told a burglar in a stolen coat that his oath was well given, and he was right, and I have never been paid a compliment I earned more completely or deserved less.
STATEMENT 35
Why did you?
Golnar cried in the stairwell for about four minutes and then stopped and was extremely embarrassed, which is the whole of my family in one sentence.

She did it with her back to everybody and one hand on the rail, and Farid stood about a metre away and did not touch her and did not say anything, which was correct, and which I want on the record as the fourth or fifth time in this book that man has done exactly the right thing without being told.
Mahnaz did not go to her either.

She stood at the top of the stairs with her bag over her arm and watched her daughter cry and did not move, and I understood — after about a minute, watching them both — that this was not coldness, it was thirteen years of practice at letting a person finish, which she has had to do a great many times about a great many things, most of them me.
Then Golnar came up the stairs and said, "Right," and wiped her face with the back of her hand and said, "Right," again.
And she said to me: "You didn't have to swear."
I said it was nothing.
And she said, "It isn't nothing. My mother told me. She said people don't do that. She said in this country you can lose a house rather than swear and nobody thinks less of you."
I did not look at Mahnaz.

I want it in the record that I did not look at Mahnaz, and that Mahnaz was standing four feet away and had told her daughter that specific true fact at some point in the preceding eleven months, and that I have never known and will never know whether she said it before the hearing or after.
Then Golnar said: "Why did you?"
And I said the only sentence I have ever said to my daughter that was completely true in both directions.
I said: "Because I knew it."
PART FIVE — A NUMBER
Statements Thirty-Six to Forty
STATEMENT 36
I haven't got very many people I can ring
I want to give the corridor.
Not the stairwell — that was four minutes and it is written. The corridor, twenty minutes later, on the ground floor, by the doors, when it was finished and everybody was going.

Farid had gone to get the car. Mahnaz had gone to speak to somebody about the written notification, which she did not need to do, and which she did because she is a woman who leaves a room when a room needs her to leave it.
So it was the two of us for about ninety seconds, standing in a corridor in a court building, with people going past both ways. She said, "I don't know how to thank you."
I said the thing you say.
And she said, "No, but — eleven months. You came every time. You didn't miss one."
I said it was on my way, which is a lie of a kind I have told perhaps ten thousand times and which is the only lie I regret from that entire day.
And then she said it.
She said: "I haven't got very many people I can ring."

Not sadly. That is what I want in the record and it is the thing that took the legs out from under me. She said it briskly, in the way you state a fact about your circumstances that you have long since stopped feeling anything about — the way you say I don't drive — and she said it while looking at her telephone to check whether Farid had come round.
Twenty-three years old. Married to a decent man. A mother she is close to. And a list of people she can ring that is short enough for her to have counted it.
I have been to a great many places in five years and done a great many things in other men's clothes, and I have written about most of them with some pleasure.

I made that. That is mine. That is the only thing in this entire account that I built myself, from nothing, over nineteen years, by a series of small correct-seeming decisions taken in bad weeks and never once read back.
And then she said the four words.
She said: "Can I ring you again?"
STATEMENT 37
She was right about the arithmetic
I said yes.

I want to be honest about the size of it, because a reader who has come this far deserves better than a man pretending that was a large moment. It was not large. It took a second. She was looking at her telephone.

But I had agreed with Mahnaz Shokri, in a car park in Tir, in eleven seconds, standing up, that when this was finished I would go and not come back and not ring her. And Mahnaz was correct in every particular. She had done the arithmetic thirteen years earlier and it is the only piece of arithmetic in this book that nobody has ever found a hole in, and I have looked.
And I said yes to my daughter in a corridor in about a second, and I did not even have the decency to hesitate.
Here is what I have worked out since, and it does not exonerate me. Mahnaz was right about the arithmetic and wrong about the alternative.
Her sum was: a man in her life who is not her father, under a false name, forever, and one day she loses two people at once and she is thirty-five.
That is correct. Every part of it. I have not found the hole and there is not one.
But her sum has another side, and it is the side you can only see if you are the one being rung. It is: twenty years of somebody answering.

And I had been two metres above a table in Mashhad six weeks earlier with the alarm switched off, and I had worked out that there were about twenty years in it, and that nineteen was not most of it. So I said yes.

I want it recorded that I know exactly what I chose and what it costs and who pays for it, and that I did not choose it in the corridor. I chose it on a table in Dey and the corridor was just the day it got asked.

And that if Mahnaz Shokri ever reads this, she will not be surprised by one word of it, because she is the only person on this earth who has ever known what I am, and she knew when she rang me on the ninth of Tir that this was how it would end, and she rang me anyway, because her daughter was going to lose a house.
She has been doing sums for thirteen years in which she is always the one who pays.
STATEMENT 38
A plan, which I have never made for anything
I did the plan on the Friday, in a rented room, on paper.

I have never done this before. I want that in the record because it is genuinely the most surprising thing in six books: a man of fifty-one who has made no plan, ever, for anything — not for the border he was going to cross in twelve days in 1404, not for what he would do after any of the six coats came off, not for one single hour of his own life beyond the next building — sat down at a table with a pen and made a plan for a relationship.
Here is what is on the paper. I have it still.

One. The number. She has a number. It is a telephone I have had for eleven months and it must not change, ever, and that means it must be paid for in a way that does not depend on me being anywhere, and I have arranged that, and it is the single most expensive thing I do.

Two. Answering. It must be answered. Not returned — answered, on the day, because a person who rings twice and gets nothing stops ringing, and the entire value of this arrangement is that it is reliable, and reliability is the only asset I have ever manufactured that was not stolen.

Three. Distance. I do not live in Tehran and I will not. A man who is available for a matter is a man who arrives; a man who is nearby is a man who is expected at Nowruz, and Nowruz is a table with people at it and a chair, and I have sat in one of those before and I know what it does.

Four. The coat. The coat is now permanent. Not a costume I put on for a purpose. It is what I wear, for the rest of it, and I have written in this account that this converts the fraud from a crime into a vocation and I am not going to soften that now.
Five. What happens if I am taken.
That is the one I spent four hours on.

If I am arrested, or if the stone finishes what it started, that number stops answering and she never finds out why, and a woman who has already had one man go silent gets a second one, and the second one is the same man.

So there is an arrangement. There is a person who has an envelope. Inside it is not a confession — I want to be clear, there is no letter in that envelope that tells her anything — there is simply a means by which she would be told, once, by somebody, that the man she rang has died. Nothing else. No name.
It is the smallest possible decency and it took me four hours and it is the only thing I have ever set up in my life for a moment when I would not be there.
Six. On the paper, in my own hand, the last line, and I do not remember writing it:
Do not be a father. Be a telephone that works.
STATEMENT 39
There is nobody to tell
I want to deal with the sheet.

It has been in a coat since the basement. It has been in that coat through a hospital, an operation, half an hour of saying my own name to a nurse, eight months of corridors, an oath, and a ruling. Forty-one entries. A third of the way down: Parvaneh Fani. Tehran. A woman of twenty-two four months gone who said the truest thing she ever said to a boy of nineteen with a notebook. Possible. S. H. Vahedi.

I have thought about what to do with it every day for a year. Golnar. No. There is no version of that conversation that does not begin with who I am, and it would cost her the man in the corridor and give her a thief, and Mahnaz did that sum in 1397 and got the right answer.

Mahnaz. I considered it for a long time and it is the only one that was ever close, because she is the only person who could hear it, and because she is owed something and I have nothing else. And then I understood that giving it to her would be handing a woman who has carried one line for thirteen years a second thing to carry, and that I would be doing it to be known, which is the only appetite I have never been able to get out of myself.

The boy. He rang twice this year from a road. He is eighteen and he has a licence in his own name now and he is doing well and he tells me about margins for eleven minutes at a time. He does not know one single thing about any of this and he is not going to, because he is the one person in the world who thinks well of me and I am not going to spend that.

Nasser Mokhtari died in Aban. His wife told me on the telephone. He was eighty-one and he had a fall and there was a fortnight in a hospital, and she said he had been pleased about the basement and had told a number of people about it, and I sat down on a step in a street when she said that.
So there is nobody.

That is not self-pity and I want it read flatly, because it is simply the position: I am the only person alive who knows what my mother wanted, and what was done about it, and by whom, and what he wore, and where the coat went.
Six books ago I put on a dead man's clothes because they were on a chair and nobody was watching the chair.

I have found out, at fifty-one, that the chair was not an accident and that the man in it was the answer, and that he had been dead about an hour, and that everything I have done since — a shrine, a clinic, a school, a prison, a house at a border, a court in Tehran — came out of a coat I took off the man my mother was sent to.
And I cannot tell one person.

That is the finding. Everything else in these six accounts was a thing I did to somebody. This is a thing that was done to me before I was born, correctly, by a boy of nineteen doing what he was told, and it worked, and here I am.

The sheet goes in the bag. The bag has in it: a comb, a tin of wire hooks, a photograph of a woman who was either somebody's mother or somebody's wife, an exercise book with thirty-one names crossed out in the back, a folded page with a name on it written four times, and forty-one entries on a sheet of ruled paper from Aban of 1357. Somebody will open that bag one day and will not know what any of it is.
STATEMENT 40
What I would do differently
She rang in Ordibehesht about something small.

I am not going to say what. It was small — it was the kind of thing you ring somebody about when you have decided that they are a person you ring, and that is the whole of its significance and it has none of any other kind.
It took nine minutes. I was useful for about four of them.
At the end she said, "Sorry, this was probably nothing."
And I said it was not nothing.
And she said, "Okay. Thanks, Haj Aqa," and rang off, and I stood in a street in a town I am not going to name and looked at a telephone for longer than a man should look at a telephone.
I have been six men.

A burglar for twenty-seven years, which was not a success. A sayyid in a salt town for fourteen months. A doctor on a dying qanat for fourteen weeks. A teacher in a gorge for four months, which is the only one I would do again. An inspector with a lanyard for nine days, which is the only one that had any power in it and the only one whose power was entirely negative. And somebody's brother-in-law for five months in a house at a border, which I left on my own decision and had never done before.

I have kept that count for six years the way I kept the six hundred doors and the eighty apologies and the eleven weeks, which is to say without deciding to, because counting is the only thing my head does on its own.
I am going to add them up properly now, once, and then I am going to stop.
Fourteen months. Fourteen weeks. Four months. Nine days. Five months.
Somewhere around three years.

Six extraordinary men, and the whole of them together comes to about three years — and in every one of those three years I was, and I am not being modest about this because modesty is a thing you can afford when you have something else, very good. Better than the men whose jobs they were. I have been told so by a nurse, by a schoolmaster, by a prison physician and by an advocate of thirty years' standing who had just lost to me.
And I could not manage nineteen years of being one ordinary man in one place for one child.
That is the finding. I have had four years to find a hole in it and there is not one, and I have looked in the way I used to look at a wall.
Here is the mechanism, since these accounts have always been about mechanisms and it would be a poor way to finish to go vague at the end.
I was excellent in those coats because every one of them had a date on it.

That is all. That is the entire trick and it is not a trick, it is a defect with good manners. I have written since the first of these that I could be an extraordinarily good man for somewhere between six and eleven weeks, and I put it down as an observation about women and was rather pleased with the phrasing, and it took me five books and an operating table to understand that I had been describing my whole life and had thought I was describing an affair.

Attention is the only thing I have ever actually owned. Not the reading, which I cannot do. Not the cleverness, which is ordinary. The one inherited thing: my mother could go into a room and know in four seconds who was pregnant and who was being cheated on and who had not eaten, and she could not write her own name, and she gave that to me and it is worth more than everything I ever took through a window.
And I spent it on strangers.

For twenty-seven years I gave four hours of total, undivided, professional attention to the contents of other people's houses. For five years I gave it to villages, wings, classrooms and corridors. I have paid more attention to a drain in a prison yard, for longer, with more of myself, than I ever paid to my own daughter between the ages of five and nineteen.
And the reason is not that I am a monster. I want that stated flatly, because the easy version of this account is a bad man being sorry, and the easy version is false.
The reason is that a stranger does not need you on Wednesday.

You can be magnificent for a stranger. You can put the whole of yourself into forty minutes in a waiting room, and then the bell goes and you are released, and you have been the best man in that building and you have promised nothing. A child needs you on Wednesday. And on the Wednesday after that. And she will need you on a Wednesday when you are tired and have nothing in you and there is no audience and nobody is going to say Haj Aqa, thank you, and that — not a wall, not a lock, not a prison — is the only thing in my life I have ever found genuinely impossible.
So: the fraud was never the coat.

I want to put that down clearly, because six books have been about coats and a reader is entitled to think that is what I have been confessing. It is not. The coats were the least dishonest thing about me. In every one of them I did what I said I would do and most of what I did was good and I am not going to take it back.
The fraud was that I gave the only true thing I had to people who would never ask me for it twice.

That is what I did. I was not a man pretending to be a cleric. I was a man pretending that fourteen months of somebody else's life was the same as being somebody, and it is not, and the difference is that a life is the boring part and I could not do the boring part.
Now the question everybody asks, and I have been asked it once, by a boy in a cab at four in the morning, and I gave him a poor answer.
What would I do differently.

Not the coats. I want to say that first and I want it on the record in my own hand: I would not give back one of them. Not the salt town, not the clinic, not the gorge, and not the prison, which cost a decent man his working life and which I have never pretended otherwise about.

The reason is arithmetic and it is not sentiment. You cannot pull one thread out of that. A woman in a village is alive and has grandchildren because a fraud with a stolen card read a stairwell in Karaj in 2004 and recognised a shape. Forty children in a gorge were warm for thirty years because a man who could not read a form went through eleven years of circulars with a child's dictionary. A doctor got, in four months, what eleven years of correct procedure had not given her. And a boy of eleven with a ledger in the back of his mathematics book found out that an adult could take him seriously, and it changed what he is, and I have seen the man it made.

All of that is in the same bundle as the boy at the ford and the nineteen pages and everything else I have done, and I have tried for four years to separate them and they do not separate. Anybody who tells you otherwise has not tried.
So I would not change a coat.
I would change a Tuesday.

There is a Tuesday afternoon in the spring of 1389. Golnar is four. She is sitting on the floor of a flat in Tehran with a plate and she is telling me a story about her food — the rice is going to the corner, the rice does not want to — and it is not a good story and it does not go anywhere, and she is telling it to me because she has decided that I am the person you tell.

And I am doing something. I have never been able to recover what. A ledger, a telephone, a thing about a man in Karaj. It does not matter and that is the point: whatever it was, it is gone, and I could not tell you one detail of it now under oath.
And I said: in a minute.
And I did not come back.

Not that afternoon and not, in any sense that would have registered on a four-year-old, ever. By the autumn she had stopped bringing me things. I noticed. I remember noticing and being faintly relieved, because I was busy, and a child who has stopped bringing you things is a child who is settling down.
That is the four minutes.

I have gone through six hundred buildings in my head. I can give you the lock on the second floor of a block in Yousef Abad that I went through in 1379 and I can tell you what the carpet smelled like. I have total recall of everything I ever stole.
I cannot get back four minutes on a Tuesday, and there is no version of this account, and no coat, and no court, and no true thing said under oath in a false name, that buys them.
And I want to be careful about the shape of that, because a man who ends an account like this one with a small domestic regret is inviting you to find him softer than he is.

It is not a lesson about crime. Men with clean records do that Tuesday four times a week for nineteen years and are considered to have done nothing wrong, and by any law they are right, and I would not want to see one of them punished for it.
It is not a lesson about being present, either, which is a phrase people use now and which means nothing, and which I have heard said by men who were not.
It is arithmetic, and it is this.

The people who need you are the ones who will not thank you for it, and that is not a flaw in the arrangement. That is the arrangement. A stranger thanks you because you were not obliged. A daughter does not thank you because you were. Everything that has ever gone wrong in my life has come out of preferring the first, and preferring it was never a decision — it was a hundred Tuesdays, taken singly, each of them entirely reasonable, and never once read back.

I am fifty-one. I worked out on a table in Mashhad, with the machinery that produces excuses switched off for half an hour, that I have about twenty years and that nineteen is not most of it. I decided in that half hour to spend those twenty years as somebody else, because that is the only door that is open, and I want it recorded that I knew exactly what I was choosing and chose it anyway and have not regretted it for one day.
It is not what I would have chosen at thirty-one.
It is what is left, and what is left is not nothing, and a man who waits until he can have the whole thing back will get none of it.
There is a poem about thirty birds who go a very long way to find a king.

I have never read it. It has been told to me five times by five people and four of them told it wrong, and I told it wrong myself to a room of children and a girl of nine stood up and corrected me out of the book, and I have thought about her more often than about most of what is in these six accounts.

There is a parrot in it. Green, with a gold collar. He is kept in a cage because he is beautiful and because he can talk, and he is fed by hand, and when the birds ask him to come he says: I do not want your king. I want the water of Khizr, the water that means a man does not die. I want more of this.
And the hoopoe tells him he is asking for the wrong thing beautifully, and that a man who is willing to die can find that water, and a man who only wants not to die will never get anywhere near it.
You have mistaken your keeper for your life.
I have thought about the parrot for a year and I do not think I am the bird who wanted to live forever. I have never much minded dying and I have been extremely careless with the question.
I am the one who thought the cage was a road.

Six coats and six exits and a count I could not stop keeping, and every one of them felt like movement, and I was extremely proud of the movement, and I have been going round and round a small bright room for fifty years being admired for the distance.
I am fifty-one. There is about twenty years in it, less the stone.
She has my number.
AFTERWARD
Written afterwards by Hamed, who was eleven in the winter of
ENTRY 1
How I found out

I have kept a book since I was eleven years old and everything in it is numbers. Loads, hours, costs, what I owe and what I am owed. My wife says it is the only diary in Iran with no feelings in it and she is right, and I have always been pleased about that.
I am not going to do it that way here. I have tried three times and it comes out wrong.
So this is just going to be the story, told the way I would tell it at a table, and if my children ever read it I would like them to hear me saying it rather than see me counting.
A man rang me in Bahman.

I did not know him. He had my cousin's number and my cousin had given him mine, and he rang on a Tuesday evening while I was still on the road and said he had a bag that he had been asked to get to me, and would I say where to send it.
I said I would come and get it.

He has a tyre place on the edge of a town four hours away that I had never been to in my life. He is sixty-odd and he took a long time getting out of his chair and he made tea before he said anything, which I have come to understand was because he did not want to say it quickly.
He said the man who lived in the room above had died in Dey. Nine days in a hospital, and it was his chest, and it was not long.
He was seventy-one.

He said the rent was paid to the end of Esfand and he was not going to let the room out until it ran out. Nobody made him say that and nobody would have known. I have thought about it a great deal since.
I asked what I owed him for keeping the bag.

He said nothing. Then he sat back down and said, "He did my wife's forms. Four times, over about two years. Hospital and the pension and something with the land. He would not take a rial for any of it and I could not make him, and I have been carrying this bag round in the van for six weeks trying to find somebody to give it to. So do not start with me about owing."

We had the tea. He talked about the man upstairs for about forty minutes and I let him, because I could see he had not had anybody to talk to about it, and because everything he said was somebody I recognised.
Then I drove home with a cloth bag on the passenger seat, and about an hour out of that town I had to pull in at the side of the road for a while, and then I went on.
ENTRY 2
The year he taught us
I want to say who he was, and to do that I have to take you to a gorge in the north-west in the winter of 1405, when I was eleven years old.

Two hundred people. One road in, which is also the road out, and in the second week of Azar the snow takes the shoulder of the pass and that is it until Farvardin. Nobody panics about this. You just know that from a certain week onward, whatever is in the village is what there is.

We had a school. Two rooms, forty children, six grades. Grades one to three in the small room with Miss Roshanak, and four, five and six in the big room, which had a stove and a blackboard that had been painted over so many times the wood had gone curved, so if you drew a straight line on it the line came out with a bend in the middle. Every child in that village grew up believing that is what a straight line does.

There had been no teacher in the big room since Mehr. Three had been promised. None of them came. A man in the shop had the keys in his coat pocket for eleven weeks and by the end of it he was offering them to anybody who came through the door.
And then a man who had come in on the last pickup before the pass shut said he could read.

He was about forty-seven and he was the strangest teacher any of us ever had, and I want to be careful to say that we did not think that at the time. Children do not think a thing is strange. They think it is how it is.
Here is what he did on the first morning.
He picked up the register — the proper one, with all our names in it in the old teacher's handwriting — and he looked at it, and then he shut it and put it on the corner of the desk.
And he said: I am not going to read your names. You are going to tell me your names. And you are going to tell me one true thing about yourself. Not a good thing. A true thing.
It took the whole morning. Ninety minutes, thirty-nine of us, one at a time, standing up.

I can still tell you what people said. Zahra said she could whistle, and then she whistled, and the room came apart for about four minutes. Mahdi said he did not like the small room. Reza said his cousin had been to Tabriz and lied about it and everybody knew.
I said my name and I said my brother had a motorcycle.
That was it. That was the whole of my true thing, and it was not even mine, it was my brother's, and I have thought about that since and it is exactly what an eleven-year-old boy would say to a room.
By the end of that morning he knew all forty of us.

I did not understand what that meant until I was much older. That school opened in 1348. In fifty-seven years no teacher had ever known all forty names at once. Not one. They came for a year or two and they knew the loud ones and the clever ones and the ones who were trouble, and the rest of us were a room.
He learned all of us in a morning because he could not read the register.
I did not know that then. None of us did. We thought he was just a man who wanted to know.
ENTRY 3
The pot on the stove
I want to tell two more things about that winter and then I will leave it, because I could go on for a very long time and this is his book and not mine.
The first is about the break.

There is a bell and there are twenty minutes and you go out in the yard, and what happens in those twenty minutes is the sandwiches. There is an order to it and every child knows exactly where they come in it. At the top there were three children whose families had a vehicle, and they had bologna from a shop in the town. Then egg. Then bread and cheese with walnut. Then bread and cheese. Then bread and butter and jam.
And at the bottom there were the ones with bread and something not discussed.

Nobody shared. I want to be clear that this is not because children are cruel. It is because a bite you take today is a bite you owe forever and there is no way to pay it back, and at eleven years old you understand that in your bones without anybody explaining it. So you ate facing slightly away from the boy next to you and he did the same, and everybody was very polite about it, and that is how it was and how it had always been.
In the third week he put a pot on the stove.

He never made an announcement. He never said it was for anybody. He made it look like it was his lunch and that he had made too much again, which he did about twice a week for the rest of that winter, and that it would be a shame to waste it.
Nine or ten of us ate out of that pot.
Nobody owed anybody anything, because it was not a gift, it was leftovers. That is the whole trick and it took me until I was about twenty to see it.
And he did not do it every day. I noticed that at the time and it annoyed me, because I was eleven and hungry and I thought he was just being unreliable.
I asked him about it years later, in a truck, at four in the morning. I asked him why not every day.
And he said: because a thing that happens every day becomes a thing you are owed, and a thing you are owed can be taken away from you.
He was right and I have used it in my own house since.
The second thing is the stove itself.

The heater in the big room had a flue that did not draw properly. The pipe was the wrong size and it sagged and where it went through the wall somebody had stuffed the gap with rag about thirty years before. On a still cold morning with the door shut and forty children in the room it did not pull the smoke out. It dribbled it back in.
Two letters had gone to the education office about it, both from Miss Roshanak, both stamped and correct, and neither was ever answered.
He got it replaced in eleven days.
I asked him once how he did it and he said you put a second name on the letter. I was twelve and I had no idea what that meant.

That was twenty-five years ago. Nothing has ever happened in that room. Every child who has sat in it since 1406 has been warm, and every one of them has grown up not knowing there was ever anything to know, and that is the correct measure of the thing and he would not have wanted a better one.
ENTRY 4
I went back
In Ordibehesht, after the bag, I drove up to the gorge.

I had not been back in twenty-four years. My mother moved us out the year after I left school and there had been no reason, and then there was no time, and then one morning there was a bag on my passenger seat and there was a reason.
The road is better. That is the first thing. It is still one road and it still shuts, but they widened the shoulder in about 1414 and you can get a truck up it now, which you could not then.

The village is smaller. Two hundred people when I was a boy; about a hundred and forty now, and most of the young ones are in Tabriz or Zanjan or further. The shop is still the shop. The man in it is the son of the man who had the keys.
The school is still open.
Two rooms, and there are nineteen children in the whole building across all six grades, and a teacher of about thirty who has been there four years, which everybody agrees is a long time.
She let me in and did not ask many questions, which was kind of her.
The big room is smaller than it was. Everybody says that about a room they were a child in and it is still a shock when it happens to you.
The blackboard has been replaced. It is flat.

The stove is a different stove now, but the flue is the one he put in. You can see where it goes through the wall because the plaster round it is a slightly different colour from everything else and has been for twenty-five years.
I stood and looked at that for a while.

Then I sat down at the desk I used to sit at, which is second row on the left and still has the short leg, and I want to write down that I am a man of thirty-seven with three children and a business and I sat at a child's desk in an empty classroom in a village in the mountains and put my head down on my arms for a bit.
Before I left, the teacher asked if I wanted to see the registers. They keep them all. There is a cupboard at the back with every year in it going back to when the school opened.
She found 1405 to 1406 for me.
Forty names in a hand I did not recognise. Careful and slow and not quite even, the way you write when writing is hard and you are concentrating on the shape of every letter.
Mine is the fourteenth line down.
And in the two columns at the right there are two numbers, mine out of twenty, and they were written by a man who could not read the names he had copied out above them.
I asked her if I could have five minutes and she said take as long as you want and went out to the yard.
ENTRY 5
The last time
I saw him once more after that winter, and I should tell it because it is the last of it.

I was seventeen and driving fuel on the border routes under a name that was not mine, because you cannot hold that licence at seventeen. He turned up at my grandmother's house in the autumn and stayed five months, and that is a longer story and not mine to tell.
Then my uncle's heart went and the route needed two men and I had one, which was me.
I asked him.

He said he had no licence and no papers of any kind and I said I knew both of those things, and he looked at me for about four seconds and asked how long I had known who he was, and I told him, and that was that and neither of us ever discussed it again.
We did eleven runs together over six weeks. They are the best six weeks I have ever had at work and it is not close.

He arranged it so that he did the driving and I did the talking at the barrier, which is the wrong way round because he was better at that than any man alive. It took me two days to work out why. If it had gone wrong, I was a boy doing what his uncle told him and he was a man with no papers who could not have been anything else anyway.
He gave me the version where I come out of it clean, and he did it in one sentence about a barrier, and he never mentioned it again.
He made me sit the licence test in Esfand. He drove me to it and waited outside for two and a half hours.
He left on the fourth of Farvardin, early, before anybody was up.

I knew the night before because he oiled his boots. He did that twice and left them overnight and I had seen him do it exactly three times in five months and every time there had been a road after it.
I got up at five. And then I did not go out.

I stood in the passage and listened to him get his things together and go out through the yard, and I let him go, because the one thing that man could not do in this world was be thanked, and standing at the top of a lane at five in the morning would have been a thanking whatever either of us said. And it would have been for me. Not for him.
I have never been sure I was right about that. I am still not sure. It is the only thing about him I would go back and change.
I put a piece of paper in his bag instead, with the name of a man in Tabriz who owed me a favour. It was the only useful thing I had.
That was the last time.
ENTRY 6
The telephone number
In the bag there was a sealed envelope with a telephone number written on the front.
On the back, in his handwriting, which is slow and careful and puts each letter down separately like a man laying bricks:
If I am not here, ring this. Say only: the man you used to ring has died. Do not say my name. Do not answer questions. Then put the telephone down and do not ring again.
I sat with that for eleven days before I did it. Not because I was deciding. I was always going to do it. I just wanted to be ready.
I rang on a Thursday at about six in the evening.

A woman answered. Forty-odd by her voice. There were people talking behind her and she moved somewhere quieter, and it took about four seconds, and I have thought about those four seconds more than about anything else in this.
I said the sentence.
She was quiet for a while. Then she said, "When?"
I said Dey.
And she said — not upset, just the way you say a thing you have already half worked out —
"I rang him in Dey. He didn't answer. I thought he was busy."
I said I was sorry.
She said, "No — no, thank you. Thank you for ringing. Nobody rings."
And then she said, "Sorry, who are you?"
And I said: "Nobody. I've just got the number."
She said all right, and thank you again, and we said the things people say, and she rang off.
I do not know who she was and I never will.
But she rang him in Dey and he did not pick up, and because he was a man who always picked up, she assumed the reason was ordinary.
So she went a month or two mildly annoyed with him, the way you are with somebody who has not got back to you.
I keep coming back to that. There is nothing to be done about it. It just sits there.
ENTRY 7
What I told my son
My eldest is nine. He is at the age where he has started asking who people were, and he asked me about the man whose bag is in our cupboard.
So I told him, and I am going to write down what I told him, because it took me a while to find a way to say it simply and I do not want to lose it.
I said: when I was your age a man came to our school in the mountains and taught us for four months, and he was the best teacher any of us ever had.
He asked why.
And I said: because he listened.
That is all of it. That is the whole thing and it took me twenty-five years to be able to say it in three words.

Every other teacher we had stood at the front with the book open and listened for our mistakes. He did not have the book. So when you stood up and recited, he listened to you — where you hurried, where you went flat, which line you leaned on — and then he would say do that line again, and you would, and it would be better, and neither of you could have told anybody why.
He could not check anything. So he had to pay attention. And paying attention turned out to be the whole job, and nobody had noticed, because everybody before him had been too busy checking.
I told my son the other things too. The pot on the stove that was never a gift. The stove that got fixed in eleven days. The forty names in one morning.

I did not tell him that the man could not read. I have thought about whether that is honest and I have decided it is, because it is not the important part, and because a nine-year-old would make it the only part.
Then he asked what happened to him and I said he got old and he got ill and he died in a hospital in the winter and a man who ran a tyre place made me a cup of tea and gave me his bag.
And my son said that was sad, and I said yes, it is, and also he was seventy-one and he had people, and that is not the worst way for a thing to finish.

The bag is in the cupboard. There is a comb in it and a tin of wire hooks and a photograph of a woman with no name on the back. There is a pair of shoes, oiled twice and left overnight, which means he had been going somewhere.
There is a folded page with a name on it, written four times.

There is an old sheet of ruled paper from 1357 with forty-one lines on it in somebody's careful young handwriting, and I do not know what it is. Some sort of form. Somebody went round asking people something and wrote down the answers. I have looked at it a dozen times and there is nobody left to ask.
And there is my grade five mathematics exercise book, which I gave him on my last day of school when I was eleven years old, as a joke, because there was blank paper at the back.
He carried it for twenty-five years and he never wrote on it.
We have started doing a thing at our table.

It was my wife's idea after I came back from the gorge, though I think she got it from me talking too much. Once a week, at dinner, everybody says their name and one true thing. Not a good thing. A true thing.
The children think it is a very funny game and they are extremely competitive about it.

Last week my daughter, who is five, stood up on her chair and said her name and then said that she does not like the dark but she is not scared of it, which are two different things and she wanted us to know she knew the difference.
And I sat there at my own table with my own children and thought: somebody taught me that.
He would have hated being thanked for it. He is not here, so I am putting it down.

Glossary
Pronunciation is given as plain English syllables; the syllable in CAPITALS carries the stress.
Attar [at-TAAR] — Farid ud-Din Attar of Neyshabur, c. 1145–c. 1221, Persian poet and apothecary; the name means perfumer, druggist. Author of Manteq al-Tayr.

ejraiyeh [ej-raa-ee-YEH] — Persian/Arabic, writ of execution. The order that permits enforcement of a judgment. The most frightening word in the language to anybody who has not had it explained. esfand [es-FAND] — Persian; the seed of wild rue, burned on coals against the evil eye. Its crackle is recognised by every Iranian. fani [faa-NEE] — Arabic via Persian: perishable, transient, that which passes away. In Sufi usage, said of the self that has been annihilated — the state is fana, and Faqr o Fana, Poverty and Annihilation, is the seventh and last of Attar's valleys. It is also, in Iran, an entirely ordinary surname.

Khizr [KHEZR] — the green one; the immortal guide of Islamic tradition who drank from the Water of Life and walks the earth still, appearing to travellers in difficulty and vanishing. What the parrot wants.

Manteq al-Tayr [man-TEGH ot-TAYR] — Arabic, The Speech of the Birds, known in English as The Conference of the Birds. Attar's poem of c. 1177, in which the birds of the world set out across seven valleys to find their king, the Simorgh, and each first gives an excuse for not going. Their guide is the hoopoe. It is taught in Iranian schools.
Panjshanbeh [panj-shan-BEH] — Persian, Thursday, literally the fifth day. The night families gather, and the night families visit their dead.

qanat [gha-NAAT] — Arabic via Persian, channel. A hand-dug tunnel bringing water by gravity from an aquifer to a settlement. sabt-e ahvāl [SABT-e ah-VAAL] — Persian, registration of conditions. The civil registry: the office that holds every birth, death, marriage and divorce in the country, in bound books, on shelves. Your existence is in that building.
sayyid [saa-YED] — Arabic, lord, master. A descendant of the Prophet through his daughter Fatimah, marked by the black turban. It can be inherited and cannot be conferred.

Simorgh [see-MORGH] — Persian, from Middle Persian senmurw. Written another way, si morgh is simply thirty birds. Of the thousands that set out across Attar's seven valleys, thirty arrive; and what they find at the end of the road, when they are at last permitted to look, is the thirty of them. Attar does not present this as a consolation. It is the last thing in the poem and it is not softened. From Middle Persian senmurw. The great bird of Persian myth; in the Shahnameh the protector of Zal, and in Attar the king the birds go to find.
sowgand [sow-GAND] — Persian, oath. Where documentary evidence runs out, the court may put the matter to a sworn statement, which decides it.
toman [toh-MAAN] — from the Mongolian tümen, ten thousand. The unit Iranians count in, equal to ten rials.
Vakilabad [va-keel-aa-BAAD] — District of Mashhad, and the name of its principal prison.
